title: Monty Hall Switch Or Stay

q: How many people do you need in a room before two of them probably share a birthday?

title: Two Eggs Drop Strategy
q: You have two eggs and a 100-floor building. What is the fewest drops that always finds the highest safe floor?

title: 100 Prisoners And Hats
q: 100 prisoners in a line each wear a red or blue hat. Each guesses their own color from the back. How many can you save for sure?

title: HH vs HT Coin Flips

title: Two Kids Probability Trap

title: Estimate Pi With Random Dots
q: You throw random dots at a square with a circle inside. How can the dots tell you pi?
a: Pi is about four times the share inside. Four times the fraction of dots inside the circle gives pi.
why: The circle covers pi over four of the square. So the fraction of dots inside approaches pi over four. Multiply by four to estimate pi.

title: Hat Check One Over e
q: Everyone hands in a hat and gets one back at random. What is the chance nobody gets their own hat?
a: About 37%. About thirty-seven percent, which is one over e.

q: You interview 100 candidates one by one, and must hire or reject on the spot. How do you maximise the chance of hiring the best?

why: Reject the first thirty-seven and only learn. Then hire the first candidate who beats all of them. Rejecting fewer hires too early, rejecting more risks losing the best.

title: Broken Stick Triangle Chance
q: Break a stick at two random points. What is the chance the three pieces form a triangle?

title: Two Sixes Takes 42 Rolls
q: You roll a die until you get two sixes in a row. How many rolls does that take on average?

title: Positive Test Still Unlikely
q: A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test is 99 percent accurate with a 5 percent false positive rate. You test positive. Are you probably sick?
a: No, about 16%. The chance is only about sixteen percent.
why: Out of a thousand people, ten are sick and about ten test positive. About fifty healthy people also test positive. Ten out of about sixty is roughly one in six.

title: Three Ants On A Triangle
q: Three ants sit on the corners of a triangle and each picks a direction along an edge at random. What is the chance they don't collide?
a: 1/4. One quarter.
why: There are eight equally likely outcomes. Only all clockwise or all counter-clockwise avoids a collision. That is two out of eight.

title: Measure 4 Liters With 3 And 5
q: You have a 3-liter jug, a 5-liter jug and a tap. How do you measure exactly 4 liters?
a: Fill 5, pour into 3, empty 3, repeat. Use the leftover two liters, then top up.
why: Fill the five and pour into the three, leaving two. Empty the three and pour the two in. Fill the five again and top up the three, leaving four.

title: Bridge Torch Night Crossing
q: Four people take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes to cross a bridge with one torch, two at a time. What is the fastest crossing?
a: 17 minutes. Seventeen minutes.

title: Poisoned Wine Binary Trick
q: One of 1000 bottles is poisoned. You have 10 prisoners and one day. How do you find it?
a: Test in binary. Ten prisoners are ten bits, enough for a thousand bottles.
why: Number the bottles in binary. Prisoner n drinks every bottle whose nth digit is one. The dead prisoners spell the bottle number.

why: Cut a one, a two and a four. Swap pieces each day, taking change back. Powers of two make any number from one to seven.

title: Two Trains And A Fly
q: Two trains 100 miles apart head toward each other at 50 mph. A fly at 75 mph shuttles between them. How far does it fly?
a: 75 miles. Seventy-five miles.
why: The trains close the gap at one hundred mph, so they meet in one hour. The fly flies for that whole hour. One hour at seventy-five mph is seventy-five miles.

title: Ten People Handshake Count
q: Ten people each shake hands once with everyone else. How many handshakes happen?
a: 45. Forty-five handshakes.
why: Each person shakes nine hands. That counts every handshake twice. Ten times nine over two is forty-five.

title: Drunkards Walk Square Root
q: A drunk takes 100 random steps, left or right. How far from the start does he typically end up?
a: About 10 steps. About ten steps, the square root of the step count.
why: On average his position is zero, because left and right cancel. But his typical distance is not zero. It grows like the square root of the number of steps.

title: St Petersburg Coin Game
q: Flip a coin until heads. The prize doubles each flip, starting at 2 dollars. What is the fair price to play?
a: The average is infinite. The average payout is infinite, yet typical wins are tiny.
why: Each round contributes one dollar to the average. Forever, so the average is infinite. But most games pay just two or four dollars.

title: Max Of Two Random Numbers
q: Pick two random numbers between 0 and 1. What is the average of the bigger one?
a: 2/3. Two thirds.
why: Each pair is a dot in a square. The bigger number averages two thirds. The smaller averages one third, and together they add up to one.

title: Two Eggs 100 Floors
q: A building has one hundred floors. You have two identical eggs. Above some floor an egg breaks when dropped. What's the fewest drops that guarantees you find that floor?
a: 14 DROPS. Fourteen drops. That's the fewest that always works.
why: Binary search says drop from floor fifty. If it breaks, you have one egg left and must test floors one, two, three, up to forty nine, one at a time. That's fifty drops in the worst case. Try jumping by ten. Drop at ten, twenty, thirty. If the egg breaks at seventy, test sixty one to sixty nine one by one. Worst case, nineteen drops. Better, but not the best. Here's the trick. Every drop you spend on the first egg should shrink the crawl by one. Drop first from floor fourteen. If it breaks, you test thirteen floors, that's fourteen drops. If not, jump only thirteen floors, so a break leaves twelve to test. Still fourteen. So jump fourteen, then thirteen, then twelve, all the way down to one.

title: Broken Stick Triangle
q: You break a stick at two random points. What's the probability that the three pieces can form a triangle?
a: 1/4. So the probability is one quarter.
why: Most people guess one half, or one third. The real answer is much cleaner, and the proof fits in one picture. A triangle exists only if no piece is longer than the other two put together. Equivalently, every piece must be shorter than half the stick. Call the first two pieces x and y. The third piece is one minus x minus y. Every possible break is one point inside this triangle. Now require x less than a half, y less than a half, and x plus y more than a half. These three lines cut out the middle triangle. Split the big triangle with its three midlines. You get four equal triangles, and the middle one is exactly the valid region.

title: One Hundred Prisoners
q: One hundred prisoners are numbered one to one hundred. Their numbers are shuffled into one hundred closed boxes. Each prisoner may open fifty boxes. If every single one finds their own number, they all go free. Otherwise, they all lose.
a: 31%. So they survive thirty one percent of the time. From one in a billion billion billion, to nearly one in three.
why: If each prisoner guesses at random, each has a fifty percent chance. All one hundred together? One in a billion billion billion. Hopeless. Here's the strategy. Open the box with your own number. Look inside. Go to the box with that number. Keep following the chain. The boxes form loops. Following the chain from your own box, you always come back to your own number. You succeed if your loop has at most fifty boxes. So everyone survives if no loop is longer than fifty. For a random shuffle, the chance of a loop longer than fifty is one over fifty one, plus one over fifty two, all the way to one over one hundred. About sixty nine percent.

title: Monty Hall Stay Or Switch
q: There are three doors. Behind one is a car, behind the other two are goats. You pick door one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door three and shows a goat. Do you switch to door two?
a: SWITCH: 2/3. Switch. You win two thirds of the time.
why: Most people say it's fifty fifty, so it doesn't matter. It does. When you picked, you had a one in three chance. The other two doors together had two in three. The host's move doesn't change that. He always opens a goat door, so the whole two thirds slides onto the one door left. Check by counting. The car is behind door one, two, or three, equally likely. Switching loses once and wins twice.

title: Birthday Paradox 23 People
q: How many people do you need in a room before there's a better than fifty percent chance that two of them share a birthday?
a: 23 PEOPLE. Just twenty three people. By fifty seven, it's ninety nine percent.
why: Most people say about one hundred and eighty three, half of three hundred and sixty five. That's wrong. Count pairs, not people. Twenty three people make two hundred and fifty three different pairs, and every pair is a chance to match. Easier: find the chance that nobody matches. The second person avoids one date, the third avoids two, and so on. Multiply them all together. With twenty three people that product falls to forty nine percent. So a match is more likely than not.

title: Boy Or Girl Paradox
q: A family has two children. At least one of them is a boy. What's the probability that both are boys?
a: 1/3. One third, not one half.
why: The tempting answer is one half, because the other child is a boy or a girl. That ignores how the information was given. List the four equally likely families, older child first: boy boy, boy girl, girl boy, girl girl. At least one boy removes girl girl. Three families are left. Only one of those three has two boys. So the probability is one in three.

title: Coin Flips HH Versus HT
q: You flip a fair coin until a pattern appears. How many flips does it take on average to see heads then heads? And how many to see heads then tails?
a: HH: 6   HT: 4. Heads heads takes six flips on average. Heads tails takes only four.
why: They look equally hard, since each pair has probability one quarter. But the averages differ. For heads tails, track the last flip. After a head you need a tail. If it's another head, you're still on a head, so you only wait two flips on average. From the start you need a head, which takes two flips on average, then those two more. That's four. For heads heads it's different. A tail after a head throws away your progress and sends you all the way back to the start. The equations give six.

title: Two Sixes In A Row
q: You roll a fair die until you roll two sixes in a row. On average, how many rolls does that take?
a: 42 ROLLS. Forty two rolls on average, six times more than waiting for one six.
why: Waiting for a single six takes six rolls on average. People guess twelve for two in a row. It's far more. Use two states. State zero means the last roll wasn't a six. State one means you just rolled one. From state one, a six finishes it, anything else sends you back to zero. Write the two equations. Substitute and solve. E0 times one thirty sixth equals seven sixths. So E0 is forty two.

title: Collect All Six Faces
q: You roll a fair die repeatedly. On average, how many rolls until every face from one to six has appeared at least once?
a: 14.7 ROLLS. About fourteen point seven rolls.
why: The first roll always gives a new face. Then it gets harder every time, because there are fewer new faces left. With k faces still missing, each roll finds one with probability k over six. So you wait six over k rolls for that face. Keep going: two rolls, then three, then six rolls for the very last face. Add them all up: one, plus one point two, plus one point five, plus two, plus three, plus six. That's fourteen point seven.

title: Secretary Problem 37 Percent
q: You interview one hundred candidates one at a time and must accept or reject each immediately, with no going back. How do you maximize the chance of hiring the very best?
a: 37% RULE. Skip the first thirty seven, then take the first one who beats them all. About thirty seven percent success.
why: Hiring the first decent one gives you just a one percent chance. Picking randomly is no better. Here's the rule. Reject the first thirty seven candidates no matter what. Just remember the best so far. After that, hire the first person who beats everyone you've seen. The first thirty seven calibrate your standards. Try other cutoffs and the success chance peaks near one over e, about thirty seven percent.

title: Gambler's Ruin
q: You have ten dollars. You bet one dollar on a fair coin flip, again and again, until you reach twenty dollars or go broke. What's the probability you reach twenty?
a: 50%. Fifty percent. Your chance equals start over goal.
why: Many people feel the odds are against them. In a fair game, the answer comes straight from the starting point. In a fair game your chance of reaching the goal is just your start divided by the goal. So starting with ten dollars to reach twenty is fifty percent. Start with one dollar to reach one hundred and it's one percent.

title: Hat Check Derangement
q: Ten people check their hats. The hats are returned in random order. What's the probability that nobody gets their own hat back?
a: 1/e ≈ 37%. About thirty seven percent, no matter how many hats.
why: Most people guess it shrinks as more people play, like one over ten. It doesn't. Count the shuffles where nobody is fixed, called derangements, using inclusion exclusion. The terms are one, minus one, plus one half, minus one sixth. That series converges incredibly fast. For ten hats it equals thirty six point seven nine percent. It's one over e, about thirty seven percent, whether there are ten hats or ten million.

title: Russian Roulette Spin Or Not
q: A six chamber revolver has two adjacent bullets. You pull the trigger once and survive. Now you must pull again. Should you spin the cylinder first, or just pull?
a: DON'T SPIN. Don't spin. One in four beats one in three.
why: If you spin, all six chambers are equally likely, so two in six. That's one in three. If you don't spin, the empty chamber you just fired is one of four empty chambers. The next chamber after it is a bullet only for one of those four. Only one of the four empty positions sits right before a bullet. So not spinning gives one in four.

title: Chevalier De Mere Dice
q: Bet one: roll a single die four times and get at least one six. Bet two: roll two dice twenty four times and get at least one double six. Which is better?
a: BET ONE. The single six in four rolls, at fifty one point eight percent.
why: Many people reason that four over six equals twenty four over thirty six, so they are the same. That's the gambler's mistake. Count the failure instead. Not getting a six in four rolls has probability five sixths to the fourth. For double sixes, a failure on one throw is thirty five thirty sixths, to the twenty fourth power. Fifty one point eight percent versus forty nine point one. One bet wins slightly more often than not, the other loses.

title: Bertrand's Box Paradox
q: There are three boxes. One holds two gold coins, one holds two silver coins, and one holds one gold and one silver. You pick a box at random and draw a coin. It's gold. What's the probability the other coin in that box is also gold?
a: 2/3. Two thirds.
why: The tempting answer is one half. The box must be gold gold or gold silver, so fifty fifty. But you're more likely to have drawn a gold coin from the box that has two of them. Count coins, not boxes. There are three gold coins you could have drawn. Two of them sit in the gold gold box. So two out of three golds come from the box where the other coin is gold too.

title: Tuesday Boy Paradox
q: A family has two children. At least one is a boy born on a Tuesday. What's the probability that both children are boys?
a: 13/27. Thirteen over twenty seven, about forty eight percent.
why: You'd think Tuesday is irrelevant, so one third, like the classic puzzle. It isn't irrelevant. Count equally likely cases. There are fourteen possible kinds for each child: boy or girl times seven weekdays. Families with at least one Tuesday boy: twenty seven. That's fourteen where the first child is one, plus fourteen where the second is, minus one counted twice. Of those twenty seven, thirteen have two boys. So the probability is thirteen over twenty seven.

title: Ants On A Triangle
q: Three ants sit on the corners of a triangle. Each one picks an edge at random and starts walking along it. What's the probability that no two ants collide?
a: 1/4. One quarter. With n ants it's two over two to the n.
why: Each ant has two choices, clockwise or counter clockwise. So there are eight equally likely combinations. If all three go the same way, around the triangle, nobody collides. That's two combinations: all clockwise or all counter clockwise. Any other combination has two ants walking toward each other along an edge. They collide. Two safe combinations out of eight. That's one quarter.

title: Coprime Probability
q: You choose two large random positive integers. What's the probability that they have no common factor other than one?
a: 6/π² ≈ 61%. About sixty one percent.
why: Start with the prime two. Each number is even with probability one half, so both are even with probability one quarter. The same logic applies to every prime p. They both share it with probability one over p squared. Multiply across all primes: one minus a quarter, times one minus a ninth, and so on forever. That infinite product is the reciprocal of the Basel sum, one over pi squared over six. It equals six over pi squared.

title: Random Point In A Circle
q: A point is chosen uniformly at random inside a circle of radius one. What's the expected distance from the centre?
a: 2/3. Two thirds of the radius.
why: Half the radius feels natural, point five. But there's more area far from the centre than near it. A thin ring at distance r has area two pi r d r. Bigger r means more area, so the ring gets more weight. Average the distance with that weight. Integrate r times two r from zero to one. That equals two thirds of the radius.

title: 100 Doors Toggle
q: There are one hundred closed doors. On pass one you toggle every door. On pass two every second door, on pass three every third door, up to pass one hundred. Which doors end up open?
a: 10 DOORS. Ten doors, the perfect squares.
why: A door is toggled once for every divisor of its number. Door twelve is toggled on passes one, two, three, four, six and twelve. An open door needs an odd number of toggles. Divisors usually come in pairs, like two and six for twelve. The only exception is a perfect square, where one divisor pairs with itself. Nine has divisors one, three, nine. So the open doors are the perfect squares. One, four, nine, up to one hundred. That's ten doors.

title: Bridge And Torch 17 Minutes
q: Four people must cross a bridge at night. They take one, two, five and ten minutes. The bridge holds two people and they need the torch. Two walk at the slower pace. Can all four cross in seventeen minutes?
a: 17 MINUTES. Seventeen minutes.
why: The obvious plan is to send the fastest person with each of the others. That costs two, then one back, five, one back, ten. Nineteen minutes. The trick is to cross the two slowest together, so their times overlap and only the ten is paid for. First, one and two cross: two minutes. One walks back: one minute. Then five and ten cross: ten minutes. Two walks back: two minutes. One and two cross again: two more. That's two plus one plus ten plus two plus two. Seventeen.

title: Twelve Balls Three Weighings
q: You have twelve balls that look identical. One is slightly heavier or lighter than the others. You have a balance scale and three weighings. How do you find the odd ball and say whether it's heavy or light?
a: 3 WEIGHINGS. Three weighings are enough.
why: Three outcomes per weighing, left heavy, right heavy, or balanced, means three weighings can distinguish twenty seven cases. Twelve balls times heavy or light is twenty four. Weigh balls one to four against five to eight. If they balance, the odd ball is among nine to twelve and balls one to eight are genuine. If the scale tips, say the left side is heavier. Then the odd ball is a heavy one on the left or a light one on the right, only eight candidates. A second weighing mixes them to split three, three, two. Each case is cut into groups of at most three, and the third weighing finishes it. Every case resolves in three.

title: Burning Ropes Forty Five Minutes
q: You have two ropes. Each takes exactly one hour to burn, but they burn unevenly. You have a lighter. How do you measure exactly forty five minutes?
a: 45 MINUTES. Forty five minutes.
why: You can't cut a rope in half by length, because they burn unevenly. But you can burn from both ends. Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end, at the same moment. After thirty minutes rope A is gone. Rope B has thirty minutes of burn left. Now light its other end. Lit from both ends, the last half of rope B burns out in fifteen minutes. Thirty plus fifteen is forty five.

title: Three And Five Litre Jugs
q: You have a three litre jug and a five litre jug and unlimited water. Neither has markings. How do you measure exactly four litres?
a: 4 LITRES. Four litres, left in the five litre jug.
why: Fill the five litre jug. Pour into the three litre jug until it's full. You now have two litres left in the five. Empty the three litre jug. Pour the two litres from the five into the three. Fill the five litre jug again. Pour into the three, which has room for exactly one litre.

title: Three Switches One Bulb
q: Three switches are outside a closed room. One of them controls a light bulb inside. You can enter the room only once. How do you find which switch controls the bulb?
a: USE HEAT. Use the bulb's heat as the second bit of information.
why: Most people think one look can only tell you on or off, so it can't separate three switches. But a bulb can tell you something else too. Turn switch one on and wait for ten minutes. Then turn it off and turn switch two on. Go in. Check the bulb. If it's lit, switch two. If it's off but warm, switch one. If it's off and cold, switch three.

title: Hat Puzzle Parity Strategy
q: One hundred prisoners stand in a line, each facing forward, seeing the hats ahead of them, black or white. From the back, each guesses their own hat colour out loud. They can agree a plan beforehand. How many can you save for sure?
a: 99 SAVED. Ninety nine are saved for sure, and the first has a fifty percent chance.
why: Without a plan, everybody guesses, so about half survive. With a plan, you can save ninety nine for sure. The prisoner at the back counts the black hats in front. If the count is even he says black, if odd he says white. That's the code. The next prisoner hears that code and sees the hats ahead of him. If the parity he sees matches, his own hat is white. If it doesn't, his hat is black. Everyone after keeps track of the hats already called. Each one can deduce their own colour exactly. Only the first one is a gamble.

title: Fox Chicken And Grain
q: A farmer must take a fox, a chicken and a bag of grain across a river in a boat that carries only one item at a time. The fox eats the chicken and the chicken eats the grain if left alone. How does he get everything across?
a: 7 TRIPS. Seven crossings.
why: Take the chicken across first. The fox and the grain can safely be left together. Come back alone. Take the fox across. Now the fox is on the far side with the chicken. Bring the chicken back with you. Leave it, and take the grain across. Now the fox and grain are together, safely. Go back alone, fetch the chicken. Seven crossings in total.

title: Poisoned Wine 1000 Bottles
q: A king has one thousand bottles of wine and one is poisoned. A drop kills within a day. He has ten prisoners to test. How can he find the poisoned bottle in one day?
a: 10 BITS. Ten testers are enough, because two to the ten is more than one thousand.
why: Testing one bottle per tester only covers ten bottles. You need each tester to drink from many bottles at once. Number the bottles in binary. Ten bits cover zero to one thousand twenty three, and each tester owns one bit. Tester i drinks from every bottle where bit i is one. Bottle five is binary one zero one, so testers one and three drink from it. After a day, read who died as a binary number. The pattern of dead testers is the bottle number.

title: Five Pirates One Hundred Coins
q: Five pirates must split one hundred coins. The most senior proposes a split and everyone votes. At least half must agree, or he is thrown overboard and the next proposes. Each pirate is greedy and logical. What does the first pirate propose?
a: 98 · 0 · 1 · 0 · 1. The first pirate keeps ninety eight, and gives one coin each to the third and fifth.
why: Work backward. With only pirates D and E left, D keeps all one hundred, because his own vote is half. With three, pirate C needs one more vote. E gets nothing if C is thrown out, so one coin buys E's vote. With four, B needs one more vote. D gets nothing in the next round, so one coin buys D. With five, A needs two more votes. A buys the pirates who get nothing otherwise, C and E, with one coin each. A keeps ninety eight.

title: Two Guards One Question
q: You face two doors. One leads to freedom, one to death. Two guards stand there: one always tells the truth, the other always lies. You don't know which is which. You may ask one question to one guard. What do you ask?
a: TAKE THE OTHER. Take the opposite of whatever door they name.
why: Asking which door is safe gets you nothing useful, since you don't know whether you're talking to the liar. Ask a question about the other guard. Ask: if I asked the other guard which door is safe, what would he say? If you ask the honest guard, he truthfully reports the liar's lie. If you ask the liar, he lies about the honest guard's truth. Either way you hear the wrong door. Both give the same wrong door. So you choose the other one.

title: Cheryl's Birthday
q: Cheryl gives Albert the month and Bernard the day of her birthday. The ten dates are May fifteen, sixteen, nineteen. June seventeen, eighteen. July fourteen, sixteen. August fourteen, fifteen, seventeen. Albert says: I don't know, and I know Bernard doesn't either. Bernard says: now I know. Albert says: now I know too. When is Cheryl's birthday?
a: JULY 16. Cheryl's birthday is July sixteenth.
why: Albert knows the month and says Bernard can't know. So the day must not be unique. Days eighteen and nineteen appear once, so May and June are out. Bernard now knows the date. Fourteen appears in both July and August, so Bernard didn't have fourteen. That removes July fourteen and August fourteen. Albert now knows too. If the month were August, two dates would remain. So the month is July.

title: Mutilated Chessboard
q: A chessboard has two opposite corners removed. You have thirty one dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares. Can you cover the whole board without gaps or overlaps?
a: IMPOSSIBLE. It's impossible. A colouring argument proves it.
why: You could try for hours, and the numbers look fine. Sixty two squares, thirty one dominoes. But there's a hidden constraint. Colour the board like a chessboard. Every domino covers exactly one dark and one light square. Opposite corners are the same colour. Removing both leaves thirty light squares and thirty two dark squares. Thirty one dominoes would need thirty one of each. There are not. So it's impossible.

title: Clock Hands Overlap
q: How many times in twenty four hours do the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock overlap exactly?
a: 22. Twenty two times a day.
why: Most people say twenty four, once per hour. But the hour hand is moving too, so the pattern is different. The minute hand laps the hour hand eleven times in twelve hours. It starts together at twelve, and meets again just after one. The eleventh meeting is the same as the next twelve o'clock, so there are eleven in twelve hours. In twenty four hours that's eleven times two.

title: Last Digit Of 7 To The 100
q: What's the last digit of seven to the power of one hundred?
a: 1. The last digit is one.
why: You can't compute it by hand, and you don't need to. Only the last digit matters, and last digits repeat. Powers of seven end in seven, nine, three, one, and then repeat forever. One hundred is a multiple of four. So the hundredth power lands on the last position of the cycle.

title: Trailing Zeros Of 100 Factorial
q: How many zeros are at the end of one hundred factorial, that is, one times two times three, all the way to one hundred?
a: 24 ZEROS. Twenty four zeros.
why: A trailing zero comes from a factor of ten, which is a two times a five. There are plenty of twos, so count the fives. Multiples of five up to one hundred: twenty of them, each contributing at least one five. But twenty five, fifty, seventy five and one hundred have two fives each. That adds four more. Twenty plus four is twenty four. Higher powers like one hundred twenty five don't fit under one hundred.

title: Sum Of 1 To 100
q: What is the sum of all whole numbers from one to one hundred, and how can you do it in seconds?
a: 5050. Five thousand and fifty.
why: Adding them one by one takes forever. Instead, pair the first with the last. Every pair adds to one hundred one. One plus one hundred, two plus ninety nine, three plus ninety eight. There are fifty pairs, since one hundred numbers make fifty pairs. Fifty times one hundred one is five thousand fifty.

title: Josephus Problem 100 People
q: One hundred people stand in a circle numbered one to one hundred. Starting with one, every second person is eliminated, going around the circle. Which position survives?
a: 73. Position seventy three. The formula is two times the excess, plus one.
why: Look at small circles. With two people, one survives. With four, one survives. With any power of two, person one always survives. One hundred isn't a power of two. The nearest power below is sixty four. Thirty six people must be eliminated first to reach sixty four. After thirty six eliminations, the next person to start a fresh sixty four circle is the number seventy three, because each elimination skips two seats.

title: Painted Cube Cut Into 27
q: A three by three by three cube is painted red on the outside, then cut into twenty seven small cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
a: 12. Twelve small cubes have exactly two painted faces.
why: Sort the small cubes by position. Corner cubes have three painted faces. There are eight corners. Edge cubes sit between two corners on an edge. Each of the twelve edges has one, and each shows two painted faces. Face centres have one painted face, six of them. And one cube in the centre has none. Check: eight plus twelve plus six plus one is twenty seven.

title: Squares On A Chessboard
q: How many squares of any size are there on a standard eight by eight chessboard?
a: 204. Two hundred and four squares.
why: Most people say sixty four, the little squares. But two by two, three by three, and bigger squares count too. Count by size. There are sixty four one by one squares. There are seven times seven, forty nine, two by two squares. Keep going down: twenty five, sixteen, nine, four, and one big eight by eight square. Sum of the squares from one to eight is two hundred and four.

title: Nine Coins Two Weighings
q: You have nine identical looking coins. One is heavier. You have a balance scale and two weighings. How do you find the heavy coin?
a: 2 WEIGHINGS. Two weighings. Split into three groups, twice.
why: Each weighing has three outcomes, left heavy, right heavy, or balanced. Two weighings give nine outcomes, exactly enough. Split the coins into three groups of three. Weigh group one against group two. The heavier side holds the coin. If they balance, it's in group three. Either way you now have three coins left. Weigh two of those three. The heavier one is it, and if they balance it's the third.

title: Mislabeled Boxes
q: Three boxes are labeled apples, oranges, and mixed. Every label is wrong. You may take one fruit from one box without looking inside. Which box should you pick from, and how do you correct all three labels?
a: PICK 'MIXED'. Pick the box labeled mixed.
why: Pick from the box labeled mixed. That label is wrong, so it holds only apples or only oranges. One fruit tells you which. Say you draw an apple. That box is apples only. Now the box labeled oranges can't be oranges, and it can't be apples, so it's mixed. That leaves the box labeled apples, which must be oranges.

title: How Many Nines Up To 100
q: How many times does the digit nine appear when you write all the numbers from one to one hundred?
a: 20. Twenty.
why: Most people say ten, one for each multiple of ten plus nine. That misses a whole group. Count the units digit first. Nine, nineteen, twenty nine, up to ninety nine. That's ten. Now the tens digit. Ninety through ninety nine all have a nine in the tens place. Another ten. Ninety nine has two nines, counted once in each group. Ten plus ten is twenty.

title: Eight Queens Puzzle
q: How many ways can you place eight queens on a chessboard so that no two attack each other?
a: 92. Ninety two arrangements, twelve fundamentally different.
why: There are over four billion ways to put eight queens on the board. Brute force would check them all. But one queen per row and one per column cuts it down to eight factorial, forty thousand three hundred twenty permutations. Check the diagonals on those, and only ninety two permutations survive. Many of those are just rotations and reflections of each other. Only twelve are truly different.

title: Pigeonhole Hair Count
q: A typical human head has fewer than one hundred fifty thousand hairs. In a city of one million people, must two people have exactly the same number of hairs?
a: YES. Yes, guaranteed. Someone shares an exact count.
why: You can't count anyone's hairs, and you don't need to. This is the pigeonhole principle. Make one hole for each possible hair count, from zero to one hundred fifty thousand. That's at most one hundred fifty thousand and one holes. One million people are the pigeons. Put each person in the hole matching their hair count. With more people than holes, at least one hole holds two people, so yes.

title: Heavy Coin Among 1000
q: You have one thousand coins and exactly one is heavier. You have a balance scale. What's the minimum number of weighings that guarantees you find it?
a: 7 WEIGHINGS. Seven weighings.
why: Splitting in half each time needs about ten weighings. That ignores a better move. A balance has three outcomes, not two: left heavy, right heavy, or balanced. Split into three equal groups each time. Each weighing divides the possibilities by three. Powers of three: three to the sixth is seven hundred twenty nine, three to the seventh is two thousand one hundred eighty seven. So seven weighings are enough, and six are not.

title: Euclid's GCD Of 1071 And 462
q: What is the greatest common divisor of one thousand seventy one and four hundred sixty two, and how do you find it without factoring?
a: 21. Twenty one, in three steps.
why: Euclid's idea: the gcd of two numbers equals the gcd of the smaller one and the remainder. One thousand seventy one divided by four hundred sixty two leaves one hundred forty seven. Four hundred sixty two divided by one hundred forty seven leaves twenty one. One hundred forty seven is exactly seven times twenty one, remainder zero. So the gcd is twenty one.

title: Primes Under 100
q: How many prime numbers are there less than one hundred, and how can you find them all without testing every number?
a: 25 PRIMES. Twenty five primes.
why: Use the sieve of Eratosthenes. Circle a prime, then cross out all of its multiples. After two, cross out multiples of three, then five, then seven. You only need primes up to ten, since ten times ten is one hundred. Whatever survives is prime. Count them: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, and so on, up to ninety seven.

title: Remainder Of 2 To The 100
q: What is the remainder when two to the power one hundred is divided by seven?
a: 2. The remainder is two.
why: Don't compute two to the hundred. Look at the remainders of small powers instead. Two, four, one, then it repeats. The cycle length is three, because two cubed is eight, which leaves one. One hundred divided by three is thirty three remainder one. So the hundredth power matches the first.

title: Sun Tzu's Remainder Problem
q: A number leaves remainder two when divided by three, remainder three when divided by five, and remainder two when divided by seven. What's the smallest such number?
a: 23. Twenty three.
why: Start with the largest modulus, seven. Numbers that leave two: two, nine, sixteen, twenty three, thirty, and so on. Among those, find the ones that leave three when divided by five. Two leaves two. Nine leaves four. Sixteen leaves one. Twenty three leaves three. Finally check twenty three divided by three. Twenty one plus two, so remainder two. It works.

title: Digits Of 100 Factorial
q: How many digits does one hundred factorial have?
a: 158 DIGITS. One hundred fifty eight digits.
why: You can't write it down, but digits are a log question. The number of digits is the floor of log base ten, plus one. The log of a product is a sum of logs. Add log of one, log of two, up to log of one hundred. That sum is about one hundred fifty seven point nine seven. Floor of that is one fifty seven, plus one. One hundred fifty eight digits.

title: Divisors Of 360
q: How many positive divisors does three hundred sixty have?
a: 24. Twenty four divisors.
why: Listing them all is slow and easy to get wrong. Start by writing it as a product of primes. A divisor chooses how many twos, how many threes, and how many fives to use. For two: zero, one, two or three, four choices. Choices multiply: four times three times two.

title: Detect A Cycle In A Linked List
q: Given a linked list, how can you tell whether it contains a cycle, using only constant extra memory?
a: TWO POINTERS. Floyd's tortoise and hare. Linear time, constant memory.
why: The obvious way is to remember every node you've visited in a set. It works, but costs memory proportional to the list. Use two pointers. A slow one moves one step at a time, a fast one moves two. Both start at the head. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer simply reaches the end. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer laps the slow one inside the loop and they meet. Each step the gap shrinks by one, so they must meet. It runs in linear time and constant memory.

title: Find The Missing Number
q: An array contains the numbers one to n, with exactly one missing. How do you find the missing number in linear time and constant space?
a: 4. The missing number is four, found in one pass.
why: Sorting works, but it's n log n. A hash set works, but it uses extra memory. There's a one line trick. The sum of one to n is n times n plus one over two. For eight that's thirty six. Add up the array. It totals thirty two. The difference is the missing number. An alternative is to XOR all indexes with all values. Pairs cancel and the missing number is left, with no overflow risk.

title: Reverse A Linked List
q: How do you reverse a singly linked list in place, in linear time?
a: 3 POINTERS. Linear time, constant space.
why: Walk down the list and keep three variables: previous, current, and next. Previous starts as nothing. At each step save current's next, point current back at previous, then slide both forward. After one pass previous points at the new head. Each node's arrow now points backward.

title: Two Sum With A Hash Map
q: Given an array of numbers and a target, find two numbers that add up to the target. How do you do it in linear time?
a: 2 + 7. Two and seven, found in a single pass.
why: Checking every pair works, but it takes quadratic time. For a million numbers, that's half a trillion checks. Walk once through the array. For each number, ask: have I already seen nine minus this number? Keep a hash map of numbers seen so far. Looking up is constant time. One pass, one hash map. Linear time.

title: Majority Element
q: An array has an element that appears more than half the time. How do you find it in one pass with constant extra memory?
a: VOTING. Boyer Moore voting finds it in one pass.
why: Counting with a hash map works, but uses memory proportional to the number of distinct values. Boyer Moore voting: keep a candidate and a count. If the count is zero, take the current number as candidate. Each differing pair cancels out one majority and one other. The majority has more than half, so it survives.

title: Count The Set Bits
q: How do you count the number of one bits in an integer, using time proportional to the number of ones?
a: n & (n−1). Count loops equal the number of ones.
why: Checking each of the thirty two bits works, but always takes thirty two steps. Here's the trick. n and n minus one clears the lowest set bit. Subtracting one flips the trailing zeros and that bit. Repeat until n is zero and count the steps. One step per one bit.

title: Is It A Power Of Two
q: How do you check whether a positive integer is a power of two in one expression, with no loop?
a: n & (n−1) == 0. n and n minus one equals zero, for positive n.
why: A power of two in binary has exactly one bit set. Eight is one zero zero zero. Subtracting one turns that bit off and every bit below it on. So n and n minus one share no bits. Any number with two or more bits set keeps its top bit after the and, so the result isn't zero.

title: Swap Without A Temp Variable
q: How do you swap two integers without using a temporary variable?
a: XOR. Three xors swap the values.
why: XOR has a neat property: x xor y xor y gives back x. So XOR is its own undo. Three steps. a becomes a xor b. Then b becomes a xor b, which is the old a. Then a becomes a xor b again, the old b. Try with five and nine. Five xor nine is twelve. Twelve xor nine is five. Twelve xor five is nine.

title: The Number That Appears Once
q: Every number in an array appears twice except one that appears once. How do you find it in linear time with constant memory?
a: 4. Four, in one pass with no extra memory.
why: A hash map counts each number, but it needs memory for every distinct value. Use XOR. A number xor itself is zero, and a number xor zero is itself. Order doesn't matter. XOR everything together. Every pair cancels to zero, leaving only the single number.

title: Binary Search A Billion
q: A sorted list has one billion items. In the worst case, how many comparisons does binary search need?
a: 30 STEPS. Thirty comparisons.
why: Linear search could take a billion steps. Binary search halves the remaining range each time. After k steps there are a billion over two to the k items left. You stop when that is one. Two to the thirty is one point oh seven billion. Two to the twenty nine falls short. So thirty comparisons find any item among a billion.

title: Climbing Stairs 10 Steps
q: You climb a staircase of ten steps, taking either one or two steps at a time. How many different ways can you reach the top?
a: 89 WAYS. Eighty nine ways.
why: Think about the last move. To reach step n, you came from step n minus one or step n minus two. One way to reach step one, two ways to reach step two. Then three, five, eight, thirteen. It's the Fibonacci sequence. Step ten has eighty nine ways.

title: Balanced Parentheses With A Stack
q: How do you check whether a string of brackets, like open paren open bracket close bracket close paren, is balanced?
a: STACK. Push opens, pop on closes. Linear time.
why: Counting opens and closes isn't enough. The string open paren open bracket close paren close bracket has equal counts but is wrong. Use a stack. Push every opening bracket. When you see a closing bracket, pop and check that it matches. If a pop doesn't match, or the stack is empty, it's invalid. At the end, the stack must be empty.

title: Why Sorting Takes n Log n
q: Why can no comparison based sorting algorithm be faster than n log n in the worst case?
a: n log n. No comparison sort beats n log n.
why: There are n factorial possible orderings of n items. The algorithm must figure out which one it is. Each comparison gives one yes or no answer, so it at most halves the possibilities. To tell n factorial orderings apart you need two to the k at least n factorial. So k is at least log of n factorial. Stirling's approximation says log of n factorial is about n log n. That's the lower bound.

title: Fisher Yates Shuffle
q: How do you shuffle an array so that every permutation is equally likely?
a: FISHER–YATES. Pick from the remaining positions only. Each permutation has probability one over n factorial.
why: A common mistake is to swap each element with a random position anywhere in the array. It looks random, but it's biased. Fisher Yates: go from the last position down. Pick a random index from zero up to the current position, and swap. The last slot has n choices, the next n minus one, and so on. That gives exactly n factorial equally likely outcomes.

title: Reservoir Sampling
q: Items arrive one at a time, and you don't know how many there will be. How do you pick one uniformly at random, using constant memory?
a: 1/k RULE. Replace with probability one over k. Everyone ends up equally likely.
why: You can't wait until the end to count them, and you can't store them all. Decide as you go. Keep the first item. When the k-th item arrives, replace the kept one with probability one over k. Check item one survives to the end with probability one times one half times two thirds, and so on, which telescopes to one over n.

title: Hash Collisions Birthday Bound
q: A hash function outputs 32 bit values, about four point three billion possibilities. Roughly how many items can you hash before a collision is more likely than not?
a: ~77,000. Only about seventy seven thousand items.
why: Many people guess two billion, half the space. That's wrong. It's the birthday paradox in disguise. A collision needs any pair to match. With n items there are about n squared over two pairs. Each pair collides with probability one over two to the thirty two. Set pairs over two to the thirty two to about point seven. Solve for n: about seventy seven thousand items. Far fewer than anyone expects.

title: Design An LRU Cache
q: Design a cache of fixed size that evicts the least recently used item when full, with constant time get and put.
a: MAP + LIST. A hash map plus a doubly linked list.
why: A plain hash map gives constant lookup, but doesn't know the order of use. A list knows the order but searching is slow. Combine them. A hash map from key to a node in a doubly linked list. The list is ordered from most to least recently used. On get or put, move that node to the front. When full, drop the node at the tail. All steps are constant time.

title: Find The Duplicate Number
q: An array has n plus one integers, each between one and n. At least one repeats. How do you find a duplicate in linear time, constant space, without modifying the array?
a: FLOYD. Cycle detection finds it in linear time and constant space.
why: Sorting modifies the array, and a set uses extra memory. Treat the array as a linked list instead. Each value points to a position. Because there are n plus one values in n slots, two positions point to the same place, so there's a loop. The duplicate value is where the loop starts. Use the tortoise and hare, then move one pointer from the start to find the loop's entrance.

title: Maximum Subarray Kadane
q: Given an array of positive and negative numbers, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum, in linear time.
a: 6. The best subarray sums to six.
why: Trying every start and end takes cubic time naively, or quadratic with prefix sums. Kadane: keep the best sum ending here. At each number, either extend the running sum or start fresh. Walking the array, the running sum peaks at six, covering four, minus one, two, one.

title: Rate Limiter Token Bucket
q: How would you design a rate limiter that allows short bursts but enforces an average limit?
a: TOKEN BUCKET. Capacity sets the burst, the refill rate sets the average.
why: A fixed window counter is simple, but lets double the rate through at a window boundary. Use a token bucket. The bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request takes one token. No token, the request is rejected or queued. Bursts are limited by capacity, average by refill.

title: Consistent Hashing
q: You spread keys over servers with hash modulo n. When you add a server, almost every key moves. How do you avoid that?
a: THE RING. Only about one over n of the keys move.
why: With modulo, going from four to five servers remaps about eighty percent of the keys. Caches go cold. Put servers and keys on a circle by hashing them. Each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Add a server and it only takes keys from its clockwise neighbour. On average one over n of the keys move.

title: Bloom Filter
q: How can you test whether an item is in a huge set using very little memory, accepting occasional false positives but no false negatives?
a: NO FALSE NEGATIVES. No false negatives, a controllable chance of false positives.
why: Storing every item exactly would take gigabytes. A hash set is accurate but heavy. Use a bit array and several hash functions. To add an item, set the bits that each hash points to. To query, check those same bits. If any is zero, the item is definitely not present. If all are one, it's probably present.

title: Nested Loop Complexity
q: What's the time complexity of a loop where i runs from zero to n and the inner loop runs j from zero to i?
a: O(n²). Quadratic. The constant is one half.
why: Many say n squared and stop there. That's right, but the real count tells you how it behaves. The inner loop runs i times on iteration i. Total is zero plus one plus two, up to n minus one. That's about n squared over two. Constants don't matter in big O, so it's quadratic.

title: Bits For A Billion IDs
q: How many bits are needed to give a unique number to each of one billion items?
a: 30 BITS. Thirty bits. It fits in a normal 32 bit integer.
why: Each extra bit doubles how many IDs you can represent. Ten bits give one thousand twenty four. Twenty bits give about a million. Thirty bits give about a billion. Twenty nine bits give only five hundred thirty seven million, which falls short. So thirty it is.

title: Why 0.1 Plus 0.2 Isn't 0.3
q: Why does zero point one plus zero point two not equal zero point three in most programming languages?
a: BINARY ROUNDING. Binary can't represent zero point one exactly.
why: Computers store numbers in binary. Some decimals, like zero point one, have no exact binary form, just like one third has no exact decimal form. So the stored values are tiny approximations. Their sum lands a hair away from the stored value of zero point three. To compare floats, check that they're within a small tolerance, not exactly equal. Or use integers, like cents.

title: The Midpoint Overflow Bug
q: In binary search, the line mid equals low plus high, divided by two, looks perfectly fine. Why can it be a bug, and how do you fix it?
a: low + (high−low)/2. Compute the midpoint from the difference, not the sum.
why: Integers have a maximum, about two billion for thirty two bits. Add two large indexes and the sum exceeds it. The sum wraps around to a negative number. Then mid is negative and the program crashes or loops. The fix: compute low plus half of the gap. Since high minus low is always safe, nothing overflows.

title: Row Major Versus Column Major
q: You sum every element of a big two dimensional array. Looping rows then columns is much faster than columns then rows. Why?
a: CACHE LINES. Walk memory in order. Spatial locality wins.
why: The arithmetic is the same either way. The difference is how memory is laid out and read. Arrays are stored row after row in memory. Reading along a row visits neighbouring addresses. The CPU loads a whole cache line of sixty four bytes at a time. Walking along a row uses every byte it loaded. Walking down a column jumps a whole row each step, so nearly every access loads a new cache line and wastes the rest.

title: Deadlock Four Conditions
q: What four conditions must all hold for a deadlock to happen, and how do you break one?
a: LOCK ORDER. Always acquire locks in a fixed order.
why: Thread A holds lock one and waits for lock two. Thread B holds lock two and waits for lock one. Both wait forever. Four conditions are needed together. Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break just one. The easiest is circular wait: always take locks in the same global order.

title: Queue From Two Stacks
q: How can you implement a queue using only two stacks, with constant amortized time per operation?
a: AMORTIZED O(1). Constant time on average.
why: Push every new item onto the in stack. That just stores the arrivals. To dequeue, pop from the out stack. If it's empty, pour all of the in stack into it. That reverses the order. Now the oldest item is on top of the out stack. Each item is moved at most once, so the average cost is constant.

title: Stack With Constant Time Minimum
q: Design a stack that supports push, pop and getting the minimum, all in constant time.
a: TWO STACKS. A parallel stack of running minimums.
why: Scanning for the minimum each time is linear. Remembering one minimum fails when you pop it. Keep a second stack. With each push, also push the minimum seen so far onto it. To pop, pop both stacks together. The top of the second stack is always the current minimum.

title: Kth Largest Element
q: How do you find the kth largest number in a huge stream, using memory proportional to k and about n log k time?
a: MIN HEAP OF SIZE k. A min heap of size k.
why: Sorting costs n log n and needs all the data. For a billion numbers that's slow and heavy. Keep a min heap of size k. It always holds the k largest numbers seen so far, smallest on top. For each new number, if it beats the top of the heap, swap them. Each update costs log k. After one pass the top of the heap is the kth largest. Time n log k, memory k.

title: Binary Trees Catalan Number
q: How many structurally different binary search trees can you build with five distinct keys?
a: 42. Forty two. The fifth Catalan number.
why: Choose a root. Say the root is key three. Then keys one and two go left, four and five go right. The number of trees with n keys is the sum over roots of left count times right count. T of zero is one, T one is one, T two is two, T three is five, T four is fourteen. T of five adds up to forty two.

title: Gray Code
q: How do you list all two bit numbers so that consecutive numbers differ by exactly one bit, and how do you generate it for any n?
a: n ⊕ (n >> 1). One line of code gives the Gray code.
why: In ordinary binary, going from one to two flips two bits at once. That causes glitches in hardware like encoders. Reflect and prefix. Take the list zero, one. Mirror it to get one, zero. Prefix zero on the first half, one on the second. Repeat for three bits. The same trick works for any n. Or use the formula: n xor n shifted right by one.

title: Paths In A Grid
q: A robot starts at the top left of a five by five grid of squares and can only move right or down. How many different paths lead to the bottom right?
a: 70 PATHS. Seventy paths.
why: Every path is a sequence of moves. To go across a five by five grid you need exactly four rights and four downs. A path is decided by which four of the eight moves are rights. The downs fill the rest. That's eight choose four, eight factorial over four factorial squared.

title: Dutch National Flag
q: An array contains only zeros, ones and twos. How do you sort it in one pass with constant extra memory?
a: 3 POINTERS. Dijkstra's three way partition. One pass.
why: Counting works but takes two passes. A comparison sort takes n log n. Use three pointers: low, mid and high. Everything before low is zero, after high is two. Look at the mid element. A zero swaps to the low side, a two swaps to the high side, a one is just skipped.

title: Best Time To Buy And Sell
q: Given a list of daily stock prices, find the maximum profit from one buy followed by one sell, in a single pass.
a: 5. Maximum profit is five.
why: Trying every buy and sell pair works but takes quadratic time. Walk once. Track the lowest price so far. At each day, the best profit selling today is today minus that lowest. Lowest is one on day two. Selling at six on day five gives five.

title: Rotate An Array By K
q: How do you rotate an array of n elements to the right by k positions in place, in linear time?
a: 3 REVERSALS. Reverse all, then reverse each part.
why: A new array would work but uses extra memory. Shifting one position k times is slow. Reverse the whole array first. Then reverse the first k elements, and the remaining n minus k separately.

title: Nim Game 21 Matches
q: There are twenty one matches. Two players take turns removing one, two or three matches. The one who takes the last match wins. You go first. How do you always win?
a: TAKE 1 FIRST. Take one first, then always complete the group to four.
why: Work backward. If four matches remain on your opponent's turn, he takes one, two or three, and you take the rest and win. So you want to leave a multiple of four every time. Multiples of four are losing positions for the player to move. From twenty one, take one to leave twenty. Whatever he takes, you take enough to make the total four.
