title: First Ace In A Shuffled Deck
q: You shuffle a standard fifty two card deck and turn cards over one at a time. On average, which position holds the first ace?
a: 10.6. About position ten point six, which is fifty three over five.
why: A guess of thirteen comes from fifty two over four. That's close, but a bit too high. The four aces split the other forty eight cards into five gaps. By symmetry each gap has the same expected size. The first ace comes after the first gap of nine point six cards, so it's at position ten point six.

title: Expected Maximum Of Two Dice
q: You roll two fair dice and keep the larger value. What's the expected value?
a: 4.47. About four point four seven.
why: One die averages three and a half. Taking the max must be higher, but by how much? Count outcomes by the max. A max of one happens in one of thirty six outcomes, two in three, three in five, four in seven, five in nine, and six in eleven. Weight each max by its count and divide by thirty six. That's one sixty one over thirty six.

title: Drunkard's Walk Distance 10
q: A walker starts at zero and takes steps of plus one or minus one with equal probability. On average, how many steps until he first reaches ten or minus ten?
a: 100 STEPS. One hundred steps on average.
why: Many guess ten, since you need ten net steps. But random steps cancel each other out. For a walk between minus a and plus a, the expected time is a squared. Distance grows like the square root of time. With a equal to ten, that's one hundred steps.

title: Three Points On A Circle
q: Three points are chosen at random on a circle. What's the probability that all three lie in the same semicircle?
a: 3/4. Three quarters.
why: Fix point P. Each other point is on either side. Think of the three points separately. For the three to be in a semicircle, one of them must be the first point clockwise with the other two within half a turn of it. For a given point as leader, the chance both others fall in the half circle after it is one half times one half, one quarter. Three leaders, mutually exclusive.

title: Three Heads In A Row
q: You toss a fair coin until you get three heads in a row. On average, how many tosses does it take?
a: 14 TOSSES. Fourteen tosses on average.
why: For one head it's two tosses. For two in a row it's six. The pattern isn't linear. Each time you get a tail, you fall back to zero. After a run of k heads, it costs you an expected amount to get one more. A general rule: waiting for n heads takes two to the n plus one, minus two.

norm: children until a boy and a girl
title: Children Until A Boy And A Girl
q: A couple has children until they have at least one boy and at least one girl. Each child is equally likely to be either. How many children do they have on average?
a: 3 CHILDREN. Three children on average.
why: The first child is whatever it is. Now they need the opposite sex. Each new child is the one they need with probability one half. Waiting for a one half chance takes two tries on average. One plus two is three.

title: Die With One Reroll
q: You roll a die and see the result. You may take it as your payoff, or roll again and must take the second result. What's your best strategy and expected payoff?
a: 4.25. Four point two five.
why: A fresh roll is worth three and a half on average. So keep anything above three and a half, reroll anything below. Half the time you keep a four, five or six, averaging five. Half the time you reroll, averaging three and a half. That's two point five plus one point seven five, which is four point two five.

title: Ants On A Stick
q: Many ants are placed at random spots on a one metre stick, each walking left or right at one metre per minute. When two meet they turn around. What's the longest time before every ant has fallen off?
a: 1 MINUTE. One minute.
why: Tracking all the bounces looks hopeless. But there's a trick that makes collisions disappear. When two ants meet and turn around, it's the same as if they passed through each other and swapped names. So treat each ant as a ghost walking straight. The worst case is an ant starting at one end, walking the full metre.

title: Rope Around The Earth
q: A rope is tied tightly around the earth's equator, about forty thousand kilometres. You add one metre to its length and lift it evenly all the way around. How high above the ground is the rope?
a: 16 cm. About sixteen centimetres, whether it's a coin or the planet.
why: Most people think the gap is tiny, a hair's width, because one metre is so small compared with forty thousand kilometres. Circumference is two pi r. Adding one metre to it adds one over two pi to the radius. So the rope rises by one over two pi, about sixteen centimetres. And it doesn't matter how big the circle is.

title: Hourglasses 7 And 4 Make 9
q: You have a seven minute hourglass and a four minute hourglass. How do you measure exactly nine minutes?
a: 9 MINUTES. Nine minutes.
why: Start both hourglasses at the same moment. At minute four the small one runs out. Flip it immediately. At minute seven the large one is empty. The small one has one minute left. Flip the large one. At minute eight the small one runs out. The large one has run one minute, so one minute of sand has fallen. Flip it. That last one minute of sand runs out at minute nine.

title: Sum Of Digits 1 To 1000
q: What is the sum of all the digits of all the numbers from one to one thousand?
a: 13,501. Thirteen thousand five hundred and one.
why: Think of numbers from zero to nine hundred ninety nine as three digit strings, with leading zeros allowed. In each of the three positions, every digit from zero to nine appears exactly a hundred times. The digits zero to nine add to forty five. So one position contributes forty five hundred. Three positions give thirteen thousand five hundred. Add the one from the number one thousand.

norm: exactly one six in six dice
title: Exactly One Six In Six Dice
q: You roll six fair dice. What's the probability that exactly one of them shows a six?
a: 40%. About forty percent.
why: Many say it's certain, since six dice and a one in six chance each gives one six on average. That's the average, not the exact chance. Pick which die is the six. There are six choices, and each has probability one sixth. The other five must not be sixes. Each is five sixths, so five sixths to the fifth power. Multiply: six times one sixth times point four oh two. That's about forty percent.

title: Collect All 13 Card Ranks
q: You draw a card from a deck, note its rank, and put it back, then repeat. On average, how many draws until you've seen all thirteen ranks?
a: 41.3 DRAWS. About forty one draws.
why: This is the coupon collector problem with thirteen coupons. The first rank is free, and each new one takes longer. With k ranks still missing, a draw is new with probability k over thirteen, so you wait thirteen over k draws. Add up thirteen over k for k from one to thirteen. That's thirteen times the harmonic number H thirteen. That's about forty one point three draws.

title: Poker Flush Probability
q: You are dealt five cards from a standard fifty two card deck. What's the probability that all five are the same suit?
a: 0.2%. About two tenths of a percent.
why: Count the favourable hands first. Pick the suit, four ways. Then pick five of its thirteen cards. That's four times one thousand two hundred eighty seven, five thousand one hundred forty eight hands. All possible five card hands: fifty two choose five, two million five hundred ninety eight thousand nine hundred sixty. Divide: five thousand one hundred forty eight over two point six million. About point two percent, one in five hundred.

title: Two Aces In A Row
q: You draw two cards from a shuffled fifty two card deck without replacement. What's the probability that both are aces?
a: 1/221. About one in two hundred twenty one.
why: Four aces in fifty two cards. The first card is an ace with probability four over fifty two. Given that, three aces remain in fifty one cards. Multiply the two. Twelve over two thousand six hundred fifty two simplifies to one over two hundred twenty one.

title: Monty Hall With 100 Doors
q: There are one hundred doors and one car. You pick door one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens ninety eight other doors, all goats, leaving your door and one other. Do you switch?
a: SWITCH: 99%. Switch. You win ninety nine percent of the time.
why: Your first pick was right with probability one in one hundred. That never changes. The host opens every other door but one, always avoiding the car. So the ninety nine percent slides onto the one remaining door. With three doors it's two thirds. With a hundred it's ninety nine percent. Always switch.

title: Three People Share A Birthday
q: How many people do you need in a room before there's a better than fifty percent chance that at least three of them share the same birthday?
a: 88 PEOPLE. Eighty eight people.
why: For two people sharing, twenty three is enough. For three, you need many more, since a triple is much rarer than a pair. Count the ways nobody shares three: some days hold two people, the rest hold one. That sum is messy but exact. Computing it exactly, the chance of a triple is forty nine point four percent with eighty seven people, and fifty one point one percent with eighty eight.

title: Binary Strings Without Two 1s
q: How many binary strings of length ten have no two consecutive ones?
a: 144. One hundred forty four strings.
why: Listing all one thousand twenty four strings is hopeless. Count with a recurrence instead. Look at the last digit. If it's zero, the first n minus one digits can be any valid string. If it's one, the previous digit must be zero. a of one is two, a of two is three, and then five, eight, thirteen. The Fibonacci numbers again. a of ten is one hundred forty four.

title: Regions From 10 Lines
q: What is the maximum number of regions that ten straight lines can divide a plane into?
a: 56 REGIONS. Fifty six regions.
why: Each new line can cross every existing line once, at different points, if no two are parallel and no three meet. A new line crossing k old lines is cut into k plus one pieces, and each piece splits a region in two. So it adds k plus one regions. Starting from one region: add one, two, three, up to ten. That's fifty six regions.

title: Divisible By 3 Or 5
q: How many whole numbers from one to one hundred are divisible by three or by five?
a: 47. Forty seven.
why: Counting multiples of three and multiples of five and adding them double counts the numbers divisible by both. Multiples of three: thirty three. Multiples of five: twenty. Multiples of fifteen were counted twice. There are six of them. Inclusion exclusion: thirty three plus twenty minus six equals forty seven.

title: Divisible By 3, 5 Or 7
q: How many whole numbers from one to one thousand are divisible by three, five, or seven?
a: 543. Five hundred forty three.
why: Add the singles, then subtract the overlaps of pairs, then add back numbers divisible by all three. Singles: three hundred thirty three, two hundred, and one hundred forty two. That's six hundred seventy five. Pairs: fifteen gives sixty six, twenty one gives forty seven, thirty five gives twenty eight. Subtract one hundred forty one. All three, one hundred five: nine numbers. Add them back for five hundred forty three.

title: Expected Max Of Three Dice
q: You roll three fair dice and keep the largest. What's the expected value?
a: 4.96. About four point nine six.
why: Count outcomes by the maximum. The max is at most m in m cubed of the two hundred sixteen outcomes. So the number of outcomes with max exactly m is m cubed minus m minus one cubed. One, seven, nineteen, thirty seven, sixty one, ninety one. Weight each by its max and divide by two sixteen. That's one thousand seventy one over two sixteen. About four point nine six.

title: Chocolate Bar Breaks
q: You have an eight by eight chocolate bar. Each break splits one piece along a line into two pieces. How many breaks do you need to get all sixty four single squares?
a: 63 BREAKS. Sixty three, whatever order you use.
why: You might plan row cuts and column cuts, and count carefully. That works but misses the shortcut. Every break turns one piece into two. So each break increases the number of pieces by exactly one. You start with one piece and need sixty four. That's sixty three increases, so sixty three breaks, regardless of how you break.

title: Diagonals Of A Decagon
q: How many diagonals does a regular ten sided polygon have?
a: 35. Thirty five.
why: From each vertex you can draw a line to every other vertex, nine lines. But two of those are sides, not diagonals. Ten vertices, seven diagonals each: seventy. But every diagonal was counted from both ends. Divide by two. Thirty five diagonals. The general formula is n times n minus three over two.

title: Trailing Zeros Of 1000 Factorial
q: How many zeros are at the end of one thousand factorial?
a: 249. Two hundred forty nine zeros.
why: Each zero is a factor of ten, which is a two times a five. Twos are plentiful, so count the fives. Multiples of five give two hundred. Multiples of twenty five give another forty. Multiples of one twenty five give eight, and six twenty five gives one. Add them up: two hundred forty nine.

title: Smallest Number Divisible By 1 To 10
q: What is the smallest positive number that is divisible by every integer from one to ten?
a: 2520. Two thousand five hundred twenty.
why: Multiplying them all gives three point six million, which works but is far too big. You only need the highest power of each prime up to ten. Two cubed from eight, three squared from nine, five, seven. Multiply eight times nine times five times seven. That's twenty five hundred twenty.

title: Arrangements Of MISSISSIPPI
q: How many different arrangements are there of the letters in the word MISSISSIPPI?
a: 34,650. Thirty four thousand six hundred fifty.
why: Eleven letters would give eleven factorial, almost forty million orderings. But swapping two identical letters changes nothing. The letters repeat: four I's, four S's, two P's, and one M. Divide by the arrangements of the repeats: four factorial for I, four for S, two for P. That's thirty four thousand six hundred fifty.

title: Seating 6 People Around A Table
q: In how many different ways can six people sit around a round table, if rotations of the same arrangement count as the same?
a: 120. One hundred twenty.
why: In a row, six people have six factorial, seven hundred twenty arrangements. But at a round table, rotating everyone one seat gives the same arrangement. Each seating appears six times. Divide by six: that's five factorial. Equivalently, seat one person, then arrange the other five.

norm: sum of the first 50 odd numbers
title: Sum Of The First 50 Odd Numbers
q: What's the sum of the first fifty odd numbers, one plus three plus five, and so on?
a: 2500. Two thousand five hundred.
why: Look at small cases. One is one. One plus three is four. One plus three plus five is nine. Each new odd number adds an L shaped layer to a square. The first n odd numbers always make n squared. Fifty odd numbers: fifty squared.

title: 15 Friends With 3 Friends Each
q: In a group of fifteen people, can each person be friends with exactly three others in the group?
a: IMPOSSIBLE. Impossible. The total of friendship ends would be odd.
why: It sounds possible, by arranging friendships in some pattern. Count the friendship ends instead. Every friendship has exactly two ends, one at each person. So the total number of ends must be even. Forty five is odd. So it's impossible.

title: Divisible By 9 Digit Test
q: How can you tell whether a number like one two three four five six seven eight nine zero is divisible by nine, without dividing?
a: YES. Yes. Its digit sum is forty five.
why: Long division works, but there's a one line test. A number is divisible by nine exactly when its digit sum is. Why? Each power of ten leaves remainder one when divided by nine. So every digit counts as itself. Add the digits: one plus two plus up to nine, plus zero. Forty five. Forty five is nine times five. So yes, the number is divisible by nine.

title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
q: Given a list of intervals like one to three, two to six, eight to ten, fifteen to eighteen, merge all overlapping intervals.
a: [1,6] [8,10] [15,18]. Three merged intervals, in n log n time.
why: Comparing every pair works but takes quadratic time. Sorting first makes overlaps neighbours. Walk through the sorted list, keeping the current merged interval. If the next one starts before the current ends, extend it. The result is one to six, eight to ten, and fifteen to eighteen.

title: Valid Anagram Check
q: How do you check whether two strings are anagrams of each other in linear time?
a: COUNT LETTERS. A letter count table, linear time.
why: Sorting both strings and comparing works, but costs n log n. Count the letters instead. Make a table of twenty six counters. Add one for each letter of the first word. Subtract one for each letter of the second word. If every counter ends at zero, they're anagrams. One pass over each word, constant extra memory.

title: First Unique Character
q: Given a string, how do you find the first character that appears only once, in linear time?
a: w. The letter w. Two passes, linear time.
why: For each character, scanning the rest of the string for repeats takes quadratic time. First pass: count every character in a hash map. For swiss: s three, w one, i one. Second pass: walk the string in order and return the first character whose count is one.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeats
q: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. For example, a b c a b c b b.
a: 3. Three. The window is abc.
why: Checking every substring takes cubic time. A window that slides is far better. Keep a left and right edge. Move the right edge forward. If the new letter already sits inside the window, jump the left edge past its earlier position. Track the biggest window you ever had. The window a b c has length three, and nothing longer ever appears.

title: Product Of Array Except Self
q: Given an array of numbers, return an array where each element is the product of all the other elements, without using division, in linear time.
a: [24, 12, 8, 6]. Twenty four, twelve, eight, six.
why: Dividing the total product by each element works, unless there's a zero, and division isn't allowed anyway. Pass left to right, storing the product of everything to the left of each position. Pass right to left, multiplying each by the product of everything to its right. Two passes, linear time, no division.

title: Trapping Rain Water
q: Given bar heights, how much rain water is trapped between them? The heights are zero, one, zero, two, one, zero, one, three, two, one, two, one.
a: 6. Six units. One pass, constant memory.
why: At each position, the water level is the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus the bar itself. Computing those two maxima for every position takes extra memory. Instead use two pointers from both ends. Move the pointer at the shorter side, because that side's water level is already known. Add the gap between its running max and the bar. Summing across the array gives six units of water.

title: Container With Most Water
q: Given the heights one, eight, six, two, five, four, eight, three, seven, pick two lines that together with the x axis hold the most water. What's the maximum?
a: 49. Forty nine.
why: The area of a pair is the shorter height times the distance between them. Checking every pair is quadratic. Start with the two outer lines, the widest container. Then move the pointer at the shorter line inward. Moving the taller side could never help, because width shrinks and the height is still capped by the shorter line. The best pair is eight at index one and seven at index eight: seven times seven, forty nine.

title: Coin Change Minimum Coins
q: With coins of one, two and five, what is the fewest number of coins that make eleven?
a: 3 COINS. Three coins.
why: Greedy takes the biggest coin first. Here that gives five, five, one. That works, but it fails for other coin sets. Dynamic programming is always right. Let best of x be the fewest coins for amount x. Try each coin. Build from zero. Best of zero is zero, one is one, two is one, three is two, four is two, five is one. Keep going to eleven: best of eleven is best of six plus one, which is three.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
q: Given ten, nine, two, five, three, seven, one hundred one, eighteen, what's the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence?
a: 4. Length four.
why: A subsequence may skip elements but must keep the order. So two, five, seven, one hundred one works. Dynamic programming: for each element, the best length ending there is one plus the best among earlier smaller elements. The lengths come out one, one, one, two, two, three, four, four. The largest is four.

title: Edit Distance Kitten To Sitting
q: What's the minimum number of single character insertions, deletions or substitutions needed to turn kitten into sitting?
a: 3 EDITS. Three edits.
why: Try it by hand: replace k with s, replace e with i, then add a g at the end. To prove three is the minimum, build a table. Each cell is the cheapest way to turn a prefix of one word into a prefix of the other. Each cell looks at its three neighbours. The bottom right cell holds the answer.

title: Number Of Islands
q: Given a grid of land and water, count the number of islands, where an island is a group of land cells connected up, down, left or right.
a: 4 ISLANDS. Four islands, in linear time.
why: Scan the grid cell by cell. When you meet unvisited land, you've found a new island. From there, flood fill: visit every connected land cell and mark it, so you never count it again. In this grid, the groups are the top left block, the single cell on the right, the middle cell, and the bottom right pair.

title: Course Schedule Cycle Detection
q: Courses have prerequisites. Course A needs B, B needs C, and C needs A. How do you check whether all courses can be completed?
a: IMPOSSIBLE. Impossible, because there's a cycle.
why: Model it as a directed graph, with an arrow from each course to its prerequisite. A valid order exists exactly when the graph has no cycle. Use topological sort: repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites. Here every course always has one prerequisite left, so nothing can start. The sort gets stuck.

title: Quicksort Worst Case
q: What input makes quicksort slow, quadratic time, when the pivot is always the first element?
a: O(n²). Already sorted input with a first element pivot.
why: Quicksort splits around a pivot. A good pivot splits the array roughly in half, giving n log n. On sorted input, the first element is the smallest. Everything lands on one side, and the split is zero versus n minus one. That gives n levels, each doing about n work. Total n squared. The fix is a random pivot or median of three.

title: Dynamic Array Amortized Cost
q: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. Why is appending still constant time on average?
a: AMORTIZED O(1). Constant, thanks to doubling.
why: When the array is full, an append copies every element. That single append costs n. But copies only happen at sizes one, two, four, eight, sixteen. The copy costs form a geometric series. Spread two n over n appends: about two units per append. So the amortized cost is constant, even though one append is expensive.

title: B-Tree Index Billion Rows
q: A B-tree index has about one thousand keys per node. How many levels does it need to index one billion rows?
a: 3 LEVELS. About three levels, so one or two disk reads.
why: A binary tree needs thirty levels for a billion rows, and each level could be a disk read. That's slow. A B-tree node holds many keys, so each level multiplies by about one thousand. Three levels already cover a billion rows. And the top levels sit in memory.

title: TCP Three Way Handshake
q: How does TCP establish a connection, and why does it need three messages?
a: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Three messages: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
why: First, the client sends SYN: I want to connect, and here's my starting number. Second, the server replies SYN ACK: I got yours, and here's my starting number. Third, the client sends ACK: I got yours too. Now both sides know the other can send and receive. Three messages are the minimum for both sides to confirm each other's number.

title: Second Highest Salary In SQL
q: Given an employees table with a salary column, how do you return the second highest distinct salary?
a: DISTINCT + OFFSET 1. Distinct, descending, offset one.
why: A common mistake: order descending and take row two. With duplicates, that returns the top salary again. Use distinct, order descending, skip one, take one. Or use a subquery: the maximum salary below the overall maximum. It returns null if there's no second salary.

title: Find Duplicate Emails In SQL
q: Given a users table with an email column, how do you list all emails that appear more than once?
a: GROUP BY + HAVING. Group by email, having count greater than one.
why: Group the rows by email, so identical emails land in the same group. Then keep only groups that have more than one row. You can't use WHERE for that, because WHERE runs before grouping. Together: select email, group by email, having count greater than one.

title: Fibonacci 40 Naive Recursion
q: The naive recursive Fibonacci function calls itself twice. How many calls does it make to compute fib of forty, and how do you fix it?
a: 331,160,281 CALLS. Three hundred thirty one million calls, versus forty with memoization.
why: Each call spawns two more, and they recompute the same values again and again. fib of two alone is computed many times. The number of calls grows like the Fibonacci numbers themselves. For fib of forty it's about three hundred thirty one million. The fix: remember each result, called memoization, or build up from the bottom. Then it takes just forty steps. Exponential becomes linear.

title: Fast Exponentiation 3 To The 100
q: How many multiplications are needed to compute three to the one hundredth power, using the fewest with binary exponentiation?
a: 8 STEPS. Eight multiplications, logarithmic in the exponent.
why: Multiplying three by itself ninety nine times works but is slow, especially for huge exponents. Write one hundred in binary: one one zero zero one zero zero. Squaring repeatedly doubles the exponent each time. Six squarings reach three to the sixty four. Multiply in the ones bits: thirty two and four. Two more multiplications to combine: eight in total.

title: Isolate The Lowest Set Bit
q: How do you isolate the lowest set bit of an integer in one expression?
a: n & −n. n and minus n.
why: Loop over the bits until you hit a one. That works, but takes up to thirty two steps. In two's complement, negative n is the bitwise flip of n, plus one. The flip changes all bits, and adding one carries up to the lowest set bit. Everything below the lowest set bit is zero in both, and that bit is one in both. Everything above is opposite. An AND keeps just that bit. So n and minus n isolates the lowest set bit.

title: Detect Integer Overflow When Adding
q: How do you check whether adding two signed thirty two bit integers will overflow, without using a larger type?
a: a > MAX − b. Compare against the maximum minus b.
why: Adding first and checking afterward is too late. On overflow the result wraps to a negative number, and in some languages it's undefined behaviour. Check with subtraction instead. The sum overflows exactly when a is greater than the maximum minus b. For negative numbers, the same idea with the minimum. This never overflows itself.

title: Stock Profit With Many Trades
q: Given daily prices seven, one, five, three, six, four, you may buy and sell as many times as you like, holding one share at a time. What's the maximum profit?
a: 7. Seven.
why: With unlimited trades, you don't need to find peaks and valleys by hand. Every rise is profit you can capture. Add up every positive day to day difference. One to five is four, three to six is three. The falls are skipped. Total four plus three is seven. One pass, constant memory.

title: Jump Game Greedy
q: Each element tells you the maximum jump length from that position. Starting at the first index of two, three, one, one, four, can you reach the last?
a: YES. Yes. One pass, linear time.
why: Trying every jump length explores a huge tree. A greedy rule is enough. From index zero, you can reach index two. From index one you can reach one plus three, four. The farthest reach is index four. If you're ever standing beyond the farthest reach, you're stuck. Here you never are, and the last index is reachable.

title: Palindrome With Two Pointers
q: How do you check whether a phrase like a man, a plan, a canal, Panama is a palindrome, ignoring spaces and punctuation, in linear time and constant space?
a: YES. Yes, with two pointers.
why: Reversing a cleaned copy works, but allocates extra memory. Use two pointers, one at each end. Skip anything that isn't a letter or digit. Compare the two letters, ignoring case. If they differ, it's not a palindrome. Otherwise move both inward. They all match, so yes, it is a palindrome.

title: Rotate A Matrix 90 Degrees
q: How do you rotate an n by n matrix ninety degrees clockwise in place?
a: TRANSPOSE + REVERSE. Transpose, then reverse each row.
why: A new matrix is easy, but uses n squared extra memory. There's a two step in place method. Step one: transpose. Swap each element across the main diagonal. Step two: reverse every row. The matrix is rotated.

title: Find A Peak Element
q: Find any element that is greater than its neighbours in an array where adjacent elements differ, in logarithmic time.
a: O(log n). Climb uphill with binary search.
why: A linear scan works, but the array isn't sorted, so it seems binary search can't help. It can. Look at the middle element and its right neighbour. If the right is bigger, a peak must exist on the right side. Otherwise a peak must exist on the left, including mid. Climbing uphill always ends at a peak. Halve the range each time. Logarithmic time.

title: Validate A Binary Search Tree
q: How do you check that a binary tree is a valid binary search tree? Is it enough to compare each node with its children?
a: INVALID. Pass down min and max bounds.
why: Comparing each node only with its direct children isn't enough. Four is less than five, which is fine locally. The rule is that every node in the right subtree must be greater than the root. Six passes, but four doesn't. Pass bounds down the tree. Each node must lie between a minimum and a maximum inherited from its ancestors. Here four violates the lower bound of five. Not a valid search tree.

title: Find The Celebrity
q: At a party of n people, a celebrity is someone everyone knows and who knows no one. You can ask does A know B. How do you find the celebrity with about n questions?
a: O(n). Linear number of questions.
why: Asking every pair takes n squared questions. One question can eliminate someone though. Ask whether A knows B. If yes, A is not the celebrity. If no, B is not the celebrity. Either way, one person is eliminated. Repeat with the remaining person. After n minus one questions, only one candidate is left. Verify the candidate with up to two n more questions. Linear total.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
q: Given an array one, one, one and a target k equal to two, how many contiguous subarrays sum to k? How do you count them in linear time?
a: 2. Two subarrays, in a single pass.
why: Checking every start and end takes quadratic time. Keep a running prefix sum. A subarray ending here sums to k if some earlier prefix equals the current prefix minus k. Store how many times each prefix value has occurred in a hash map, starting with zero seen once. At prefix two, zero was seen. At prefix three, one was seen. That's two matches.

title: Sum Of The First 10 Squares
q: What is one squared plus two squared plus three squared, all the way up to ten squared, and what's the formula?
a: 385. Three hundred eighty five.
why: You can add them one at a time, but there's a closed form for any n. For n equal to ten: ten times eleven times twenty one. Divide by six: three hundred eighty five. Check with a quick sum: one, five, fourteen, thirty, fifty five, and on up to three eighty five.

title: Is 28 A Perfect Number
q: A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors, the divisors less than itself. Is twenty eight perfect?
a: PERFECT. Yes, twenty eight is perfect.
why: List the divisors of twenty eight smaller than itself: one, two, four, seven, fourteen. Add them.
